name: Buoyancy experiment
seoDesc: Buoyancy experiment: work out buoyant force (F₁) from the mass and the density. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the mass, the density, the gravitational acceleration and the submerged volume and the Buoyancy experiment calculator solves for buoyant force (F₁). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the Buoyancy experiment calculator work?
sections.html:
The Buoyancy experiment calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports buoyant force (F₁) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the mass (m), the density (ρ₂), the gravitational acceleration (g) and the submerged volume (V₂).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in grams. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 10 options, such as salt water (10% salinity), salt water (15% salinity) and salt water (20% salinity). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilograms per cubic meter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in gravitational acc. on Earth. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in cubic centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 40 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Buoyancy experiment calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Buoyant force (F₁)=density (ρ₁) × gravitational acceleration (g) × submerged volume (V₁)
Buoyant force (F₂)=density (ρ₂) × gravitational acceleration (g) × submerged volume (V₂)
Ball radius (r)=(1 ÷ 2) × (6) × (ball volume (V)) ÷ (PI)
Ball radius (r)=(1 ÷ 3) × height (h) + submerged volume (V₂) ÷ (PI × (height (h) ^ 2))
Ball volume (V)=submerged volume (V₁) + submerged volume (V₂)
Ball radius (r)=(1 ÷ 2) × diameter (d)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Mass, opening in grams
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Volume, opening in cubic centimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Buoyancy experiment calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the mass, the density and the gravitational acceleration — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Buoyancy experiment calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns buoyant force (F₁), derived from the mass, the density and the gravitational acceleration. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Buoyancy experiment calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the mass, the density, the gravitational acceleration and the submerged volume, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter diameter (d) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Diameter (d) opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Density (ρ₁) = 0 kg/m³. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Buoyancy experiment calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
